strengths: Practical and timely problem: Selecting the optimal combination of pretrained vision encoders and language backbones for downstream multimodal tasks is a major challenge for practitioners due to the high cost of training cross-modal alignment from scratch.

Significant empirical effort: The authors conducted an exhaustive grid search over 49 candidate combinations (7 vision encoders × 7 LLMs) across six diverse downstream benchmarks, investing over 5,000 GPU hours to establish a reliable ground-truth ranking.

Cohesive system design: Combining representation clustering (Minibatch CKA), multi-fidelity pruning (Successive Halving Algorithm), and power-law scaling extrapolation effectively targets both candidate space reduction and per-candidate training time reduction.

Strong performance vs. exhaustive search: Mordal achieves an 8.9× to 11.6× speedup over grid search while successfully retrieving the top-1 candidate in 5 out of 6 tasks and demonstrating high ranking correlation (Kendall's τ between 0.76 and 0.96).
weaknesses: Absence of simple heuristic baselines: The paper compares Mordal primarily against exhaustive grid search. It lacks comparisons against straightforward unimodal heuristics, such as selecting combinations based on standalone benchmark performance (e.g., ImageNet zero-shot/retrieval accuracy for vision encoders and MMLU/AlpacaEval for LLMs), or standard AutoML baselines such as pure Hyperband / Bayesian Optimization.

Absolute search cost remains substantial: While an order-of-magnitude reduction compared to full grid search is significant, 450–600 GPU hours per target task remains out of reach for many individual practitioners or resource-constrained teams seeking model selection for a single task.

Clustering sensitivity and projector warm-up details: The LLM clustering stage relies on passing medoid visual representations through a 'warmed-up feature projector'. Appendix C mentions a warmup round of 10, but lacks critical details regarding the training data, exact training steps, and potential biases introduced toward specific architectures during this warm-up.

Relatively constrained candidate space: The evaluation explores 49 candidates, all centered around 7B-parameter decoder-only LLMs and ViT-based visual encoders. How the clustering and scaling laws generalize across differing model scales (e.g., 1B to 70B) or architectural paradigms is acknowledged in the discussion but remains unverified experimentally.

Minor presentation inconsistencies: In Section 4.2 (page 7), the text refers to Table 3 when discussing the speedup and accuracy comparison across six datasets, whereas the corresponding data is presented in Table 2.

strengths: Addresses an important, highly practical, and computationally expensive problem: selecting the optimal combination of vision encoder and language model for vision-language models (VLMs) tailored to downstream tasks.

The proposed framework is technically sensible, effectively combining representation similarity clustering (CKA) with multi-fidelity evaluation (Successive Halving) and observational scaling laws to prune and predict model quality.

Conducts an extensive empirical validation by running exhaustive grid search over a 7x7 (49 candidates) model matrix across six diverse benchmarks, providing a solid, rare ground-truth benchmark requiring thousands of GPU hours.
Achieves impressive speedups (8.9x to 11.6x reduction in GPU hours) while identifying the top-1 candidate in 5 out of 6 benchmarks and maintaining high Kendall rank correlations.
weaknesses: Lacks direct comparisons against standard multi-fidelity hyperparameter optimization / neural architecture search baselines, such as pure ASHA, Hyperband, or BOHB applied across all candidates without CKA clustering.

The language model clustering relies on a 'warmed-up' feature projector (10 warmup steps); the stability and sensitivity of CKA activations with respect to different warmup schedules or random initializations are not thoroughly analyzed.

The search space evaluated is relatively constrained (49 candidates, all 7B-class LLMs), leaving open questions regarding how well the clustering thresholds and scaling predictions generalize to larger model families (e.g., 13B-70B) or much larger candidate pools.

On more specialized tasks such as ChartQA, the framework fails to recover the top candidate (DFN5B-Qwen at 18.6% vs. ground-truth CLIP-Qwen at 20.2%), indicating potential vulnerabilities when domain data diverges significantly from standard pretraining distributions.

strengths: Addresses an important, timely, and computationally expensive problem in modern multimodal deep learning: selecting optimal vision encoder and language model combinations without exhaustive combinatorial training.

Solid and well-rounded system formulation that attacks the problem from two complementary angles: pruning the candidate space via representation clustering (two-step CKA) and pruning per-candidate training time via multi-fidelity early stopping (SHA) and log-linear scaling extrapolation.

Extensive and compute-intensive empirical validation: the authors actually performed full grid search over 49 model combinations across six diverse benchmarks (consuming thousands of GPU hours), providing solid ground truth to rigorously benchmark search acceleration and ranking fidelity (Kendall's tau).
Detailed ablation studies and sensitivity analyses examining the individual contributions of representation clustering, early stopping, and scaling prediction, along with hyperparameter sensitivity.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental, as the core components (Minibatch CKA, Successive Halving / SHA, and log-linear scaling law extrapolation) are established tools adapted and combined into a pipeline rather than fundamentally new methodologies.

The search space is restricted in scope: experiments focus exclusively on combinations of 7 vision encoders and 7 LLMs all constrained around the ~7B parameter scale, leaving open whether the clustering dynamics and scaling laws generalize across orders of magnitude in model size (e.g., 1B to 70B).

On more challenging datasets (e.g., ChartQA), the clustering heuristic is less decisive, leading to singleton clusters, lower ranking correlation (tau = 0.76), and sub-optimal top-1 model selection (18.6% vs 20.2% for grid search).

The evaluation relies entirely on the LLaVA-1.5 instruction alignment recipe with an MLP projector and LoRA; the sensitivity of model selection to differing alignment data distributions or alternative cross-modal connector architectures (e.g., cross-attention, resamplers) is not explored.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: selecting optimal pretrained vision encoders and LLMs for task-specific VLMs, where existing zero-shot transferability metrics fail due to the necessity of multimodal alignment.

Comprehensive empirical ground truth: The authors painstakingly ran exhaustive grid searches across 49 candidate pairs over 7 diverse benchmark datasets, establishing authentic performance upper bounds and realistic speedup comparisons.

Cohesive and well-engineered pipeline: The framework effectively combines CKA-based representation clustering to reduce the candidate space with early stopping (Successive Halving) and observational scaling law prediction to cut evaluation time per candidate.

Thorough evaluation and ablations: The manuscript provides extensive analyses, including runtime breakdowns, hyperparameter sensitivity, scaling behavior validation, and extension to smaller models and alternative projector types (Q-former).
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The core building blocks—Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) for representation similarity, Successive Halving (SHA) for multi-fidelity search, and log-linear scaling extrapolation—are existing methods composed into a practical system rather than newly proposed algorithms.

Search space scope: While running 49 combinations exhaustively is computationally demanding for benchmarking, real-world model selection often spans a much wider variety of model families, context lengths, image resolutions, and projector designs.

Pruning risk on complex tasks: On ChartQA, Mordal failed to find the true top-1 candidate (achieving 18.6% vs. 20.2%), highlighting that early stopping and clustering heuristics can discard specialized candidates when performance differences are subtle or alignment dynamics deviate from simple log-linear scaling.

strengths: Practical and timely problem formulation: As open-source vision encoders and LLMs proliferate, selecting the optimal combination for task-specific VLM construction is critical yet prohibitively expensive via brute-force exploration.

Well-engineered and principled framework: The proposed pipeline sensibly decomposes the problem by combining representation-level clustering (via CKA) to prune the combinatorial space, Successive Halving (SHA) for aggressive early pruning of cluster medoids, and log-linear scaling prediction to extrapolate full-data performance without full training.

Rigorous ground-truth evaluation: The authors performed full grid searches across 49 VLM combinations (7 vision encoders × 7 LLMs) across 7 benchmarks, providing concrete and convincing ground-truth data against which search speedup and ranking correlation (Kendall's τ) are measured.

Comprehensive experimental analysis: The paper includes meaningful ablations of each component (clustering, SHA, scaling law extrapolation), sensitivity analysis over clustering/pruning hyperparameters, evaluation across different model scales, and validation across both MLP and Q-former projection architectures.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: The individual building blocks—minibatch CKA, successive halving, and power-law scaling prediction—are well-known techniques. The primary contribution lies in their integration and empirical validation specifically for VLM component selection.

Clustering dependence on the warmed-up projector: The language model clustering step requires feeding image representations through a projector warmed up for only a few iterations (e.g., 10 steps). The stability and sensitivity of CKA similarity to random seed initialization or optimization noise in this brief warm-up phase are not fully explored.

Search space scope: While a 7×7 candidate pool is computationally demanding to fully benchmark, real-world model zoos contain many more variants with varying patch sizes, resolutions, and architectures. Clarifying how search time scales when expanding the candidate pool to dozens of encoders and LLMs would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Practical and timely problem: With the rapid proliferation of open-source vision encoders and LLMs, choosing an optimal combination for a downstream multimodal task is a real engineering and research challenge.

Substantial empirical effort: Exhaustively training all 49 vision-language pairs (7 vision encoders × 7 LLMs) across multiple downstream benchmarks to establish a true grid-search ground truth requires extensive computational investment and provides valuable benchmark data.

Sensible system design: Mordal logically integrates representation similarity clustering (CKA), multi-fidelity early stopping (SHA), and observational scaling law extrapolation to reduce the search space and candidate training time.
Comprehensive empirical analysis across diverse multimodal benchmarks (Visual QA, Document QA, Knowledge QA, MMMU), demonstrating consistent speedups of 8.9×–11.6× over exhaustive grid search.
weaknesses: Missing critical ablation on candidate clustering: Figure 7 ablates early stopping and scaling prediction, but does not evaluate a baseline that removes candidate clustering altogether (i.e., running multi-fidelity search / SHA and scaling prediction directly on all 49 candidates). It remains unclear how much efficiency and ranking accuracy gain is attributable to CKA clustering versus standard multi-fidelity exploration alone.

Absence of modern multi-fidelity AutoML/NAS baselines: The comparison is restricted to classification-oriented transferability metrics (EMMS, LogME, LEEP, NLEEP), which naturally struggle in cross-modal generative settings. The paper lacks comparisons against standard multi-fidelity hyperparameter optimization / neural architecture search baselines, such as ASHA, Hyperband, or BOHB.

High absolute search cost for practical downstream adoption: While achieving ~10× speedup over exhaustive grid search, the method still requires ~470–600 GPU hours (on A40 GPUs) solely for model selection. For most practical practitioners, fine-tuning an established, high-performing generalist open-source VLM (e.g., Qwen2-VL, InternVL2) directly on the target task takes significantly fewer compute resources.

Heuristic nature of two-step clustering: Using a 10-step projector warmup with a single medoid vision encoder to extract representations for clustering LLMs is highly heuristic. The sensitivity of downstream rankings to the choice of the medoid and projector warmup duration is not rigorously explored.

Relatively narrow architectural search space: The exploration is constrained to 7B-scale decoder-only models and 2-layer MLP projectors. Critical factors in modern VLMs—such as dynamic resolution / AnyRes image splitting, model size trade-offs (e.g., 2B vs. 7B vs. 14B), and diverse vision-text connection topologies—are not incorporated into the search space.
